title: Mole Concept and Stoichiometry
scope_note: C04.01–.02 SCOPE_REVIEW; C04.05–.06 EXTENSION; mathematical complexity not evidence of official compulsory syllabus
introduction: Chemistry becomes quantitative when we connect mass, particle counts and balanced equations. Every calculation begins with a careful definition of what is counted and ends with a conservation check. We distinguish stoichiometric ideal predictions from real experimental outcomes.

subtopics.title: Mole as a counting unit (scope check)
subtopics.entry_question: What does 'one mole' mean, and why should chemists need a counting unit larger than a dozen?
core1a_paragraphs: Chemists cannot individually count atoms in a macroscopic sample. A mole is the SI unit for amount of substance, containing exactly 6.02214076 × 10²³ specified elementary entities. The 'specified' part matters: one mole of O₂ molecules contains two moles of O atoms.

An amount in moles is not itself a mass. Molar mass connects amount of substance to mass: n=m/M when m and M are expressed in compatible units. This makes counts of molecules accessible through a balance.

An ordinary classroom stoichiometry task should state the counted entity. One mole of NaCl formula units is a convenient chemical amount description, although a NaCl crystal is not made from separate small NaCl molecules.
subtopics.representation: Show a three-column count ladder: mass in grams ↔ moles ↔ elementary entities; labels specify H₂O molecules, Na⁺ ions or NaCl formula units.

worked_example.problem: How many water molecules are present in 0.50 mol of H₂O?
steps: A mole contains the Avogadro constant N_A of specified entities.
The number of H atoms in those molecules is twice as large.
worked_example.check: Less than one mole must correspond to fewer than N_A molecules.

misconception.wrong: A mole means exactly one gram of any substance.
misconception.why: The molar mass varies with the species.
misconception.repair: Always distinguish amount, particle count and mass.

subtopics.source_notes: Quantitative mole arithmetic explicitly SCOPE_REVIEW relative to the detailed secondary syllabus.

deep_dive.big_idea: A mole is a deliberately large counting unit, like a dozen but fixed to an enormous exact number of specified entities. It is not a gram, an atom or a molecule by itself. Confusion disappears when the counted entity is named: one mole of water molecules corresponds to twice as many hydrogen atoms.
reasoning_path: Define the entity before counting: atoms, molecules, ions or formula units are different choices.
Use N=nN_A to connect a mole amount to an entity count; numerical answers should include which entity is counted.
For a molecular formula, multiply molecule amount by elemental subscripts to obtain amounts of constituent atoms.
Confirm whether the problem is about a bulk sample of a substance, a hypothetical ionic ratio or free ions in solution.

discovery.title: One mole of molecules is not one mole of atoms
discovery.setup: Imagine conceptual packages containing equal numbers of O₂ and H₂O molecules, each package containing exactly one mole of molecules.
discovery.predict: Which package contains more atoms, and can either be described accurately as one mole of individual atoms?
discovery.observation: One mole O₂ molecules comprises two moles of atoms, while one mole H₂O molecules comprises three moles of atoms.
discovery.interpretation: The chemical formula supplies a multiplicity that must be applied after naming the counted entity.
discovery.limits: Mole-count arithmetic does not itself say the species are stable, pure or completely dissociated under every condition.

deep_dive.connection: Molar mass supplies the bridge between chemical amounts and what a laboratory balance actually measures.

subtopics.title: Mass, number of particles and molar mass (scope check)
subtopics.entry_question: If a tiny number of water molecules weighs almost nothing, why does a mole of them weigh about 18 grams?
core1a_paragraphs: Relative atomic masses give the mass contribution of the atoms in a formula. Molar mass expresses mass per mole of specified entities. Water has 2 hydrogens and 1 oxygen, so approximately M(H₂O) = 2(1)+16=18 g/mol.
The conversions n=m/M and N=nN_A are a bridge between scales. Use the correct identity for each substance: oxygen gas is O₂ with 32 g/mol, while one mole of oxygen atoms has about 16 g mass.
Unit analysis can expose major errors. A mass divided by a molar mass gives moles; multiplying moles by molar mass gives grams; multiplying moles by Avogadro's constant gives a count, not grams.
subtopics.representation: One mole ladder with arrows g / (g mol⁻¹) → mol and mol × (entities mol⁻¹) → entities. Specify masses are approximate when using rounded atomic masses.

worked_example.problem: Find the moles in 9 g water and its approximate molecule count.
worked_example.check: The resulting molecular count is half the count in a mole.

misconception.wrong: Use water's formula mass 18 as the number of molecules in one gram.
misconception.why: Mass units and amount of substance are different physical quantities.
misconception.repair: Write the full unit alongside each numerical value.

deep_dive.big_idea: A measured mass becomes a count of chemical entities only after a molar mass is supplied. The same element can appear in molecules, ions or compounds with entirely different molar masses, and a chemical formula must be interpreted before any conversion is attempted.
reasoning_path: Read the exact formula and calculate its molar mass by summing each atomic contribution.
Divide measured mass by molar mass with units, obtaining an amount in moles.
Multiply by Avogadro's constant only when an entity count is actually required.
Perform an order-of-magnitude check: half the molar mass of a sample should give approximately half a mole of that species.

discovery.title: Oxygen atoms versus oxygen molecules
discovery.setup: Compare 16 g of individual oxygen atoms in a hypothetical collection with 16 g of O₂ molecules in a gas cylinder.
discovery.predict: Do these samples contain the same number of counted entities?
discovery.observation: 16 g O atoms is about 1 mol O atoms; 16 g O₂ is about 0.5 mol O₂ molecules.
discovery.interpretation: Counting depends on chemical species identity and the chosen entity, not just the element name.
discovery.limits: A cylinder containing O₂ molecules should not be mistaken for free atomic oxygen; the individual-atom sample is a conceptual comparison.

deep_dive.connection: Once masses are converted to amounts, balanced equations supply the exact ideal reaction ratios.

subtopics.title: Balancing reaction equations and mole ratios
subtopics.entry_question: Why must coefficients change when balancing a chemical equation, but subscripts must not?
core1a_paragraphs: A chemical equation represents both chemical identities and the relative numbers of reacting entities. Subscripts belong to a species' identity; coefficients count how many units take part.

Balancing ensures the same number of atoms of each element on both sides. A balanced equation also defines the stoichiometric mole ratio for the reaction as written, assuming that reaction occurs as specified.

For hydrogen combustion, 2H₂ + O₂ → 2H₂O means two moles hydrogen molecules react with one mole oxygen molecules to produce two moles water molecules. It does not mean every real experiment reaches completion or contains exactly those amounts initially.
subtopics.representation: Draw two H₂ plus one O₂ producing two H₂O. Colour-match each hydrogen and oxygen atom across the arrow.

worked_example.problem: Balance Al + O₂ → Al₂O₃ and state the aluminium-to-oxygen mole ratio.
steps: Product has two Al and three O per formula unit.
Use 2Al₂O₃ so oxygen count becomes 6, achievable with 3O₂.
Aluminium count on product side is 4; use 4Al.

misconception.wrong: Change product Al₂O₃ into AlO to make smaller coefficients.
misconception.why: AlO would denote a different chemical composition.
misconception.repair: Keep species fixed and balance with integer coefficients.

deep_dive.big_idea: Balanced equations connect two languages. An equation is first a claim that every element is conserved; once balanced, its coefficients also provide ratios of reacting molecular or formula units and corresponding mole amounts. Subscripts cannot be adjusted as a shortcut because they name different species.
reasoning_path: Verify the actual reactant and product chemical identities before balancing.
Balance atoms element by element by multiplying full formulas with coefficients.
Read the resulting coefficients as a ratio of chemical amounts for the reaction as written.
Check that the ratios refer to amounts reacted or formed—not automatically every amount initially put in the vessel.

discovery.title: From particle sketch to equation
discovery.setup: Draw two H₂ molecules and one O₂ molecule. Rearrange the four H and two O atoms into water molecule drawings, conserving all atom identities.
discovery.predict: How many H₂O molecules can the picture produce without leftovers?
discovery.observation: Two water molecules contain exactly the required four hydrogen and two oxygen atoms.
discovery.interpretation: The same count becomes 2H₂+O₂→2H₂O and the mole ratio 2:1:2.
discovery.limits: A balanced representation is a stoichiometric relationship, not evidence that any mixing condition produces complete combustion.

deep_dive.connection: The next step turns mole ratios into reactant and product masses, using a separate molar mass for each chemical species.

subtopics.title: Reaction composition and mass relationships
subtopics.entry_question: Why do two grams of hydrogen gas and sixteen grams of oxygen gas not necessarily make eighteen grams of water?
core1a_paragraphs: Chemical combination follows balanced atom ratios, not arbitrary total mass. Hydrogen and oxygen gases react as 2H₂ + O₂ → 2H₂O. To find whether reagents are in the correct proportions, convert their masses into moles first.

Use M(H₂)=2 g/mol and M(O₂)=32 g/mol. The required mass ratio for complete consumption is 4 g H₂ to 32 g O₂, or 1:8 by mass. In a closed system, the initial total mass equals the masses of product and leftovers combined.
Mass-conservation and stoichiometric calculation are different but compatible constraints. The first checks the total; the second determines how much of each product or leftover species exists.
subtopics.representation: Reaction ledger with rows initial moles, reacted moles, remaining moles, produced moles. Separate masses and moles.

worked_example.problem: React 4 g H₂ with 32 g O₂ and assume complete reaction.
steps: Ratio 2:1 exactly matches the balanced equation.
No unreacted reagent remains in the ideal model.
worked_example.check: 4 g H₂ + 32 g O₂ = 36 g H₂O, consistent with mass conservation for the closed reaction.

misconception.wrong: Simply add reagent masses and assign the sum to product even when one reagent is in excess.
misconception.why: Any unreacted material is part of final mass and must be deducted from product mass.
misconception.repair: Compute reacted moles first; then convert to product mass.

deep_dive.big_idea: Mass conservation is always compatible with the correct stoichiometric result, but it cannot replace the stoichiometric calculation. If one reactant is present in excess, the final mass includes unused material and reaction products; it does not all become the desired product.
reasoning_path: Convert each starting mass to moles using the appropriate substance's molar mass.
Apply the coefficient ratios to determine the amount consumed or produced.
Convert the relevant product mole amount to grams and keep unreacted masses as separate ledger entries.
Check that total input mass equals total product plus leftover mass for a closed ideal model.

discovery.title: The 4 g plus 16 g puzzle
discovery.setup: A hypothetical vessel initially contains 4 g H₂ and 16 g O₂ and forms water according to 2H₂+O₂→2H₂O, under ideal completion conditions.
discovery.predict: Should all 20 g automatically be labelled water, or should a reagent remain?
discovery.observation: The oxygen provides only 0.5 mol O₂, consuming 1 mol H₂ (2 g) and forming 1 mol H₂O (18 g). The other 2 g H₂ remains.
discovery.interpretation: The conservation ledger balances 20 g initial against 18 g water plus 2 g unreacted hydrogen.
discovery.limits: A real reaction may be incomplete or hazardous; this is calculation-only and assumes a closed single-reaction system.

deep_dive.connection: C04's extension asks how to predict the leftover reagent directly from the initial amounts.

subtopics.title: Limiting reactants and excess (extension)
subtopics.entry_question: What makes a reagent limiting, and why isn't the one with fewer grams necessarily the limiting one?
core1a_paragraphs: A limiting reactant is used up first if a specified reaction proceeds as modeled. Its available quantity compared with its coefficient determines how many complete reaction 'sets' can take place.

For aA + bB → products, compare n(A)/a and n(B)/b. The smaller nonnegative value limits the reaction extent, under ideal single-reaction and completion assumptions. The other reagent may be in excess.

The method gives a model, not a guarantee of actual chemical yield. Reaction rates, side reactions, equilibrium and incomplete mixing can change observations; separate the stoichiometric maximum from an experimental outcome.
subtopics.representation: Use a two-column ledger of available moles/coefficient for reactants and a product yield arrow determined by the smaller extent.

worked_example.problem: 5 mol H₂ and 2 mol O₂ react by 2H₂ + O₂ →2H₂O. Identify limiting reagent.
steps: H₂ consumed 4 mol, remaining 1 mol; water formed 4 mol.
worked_example.result: O₂ limiting; 4 mol H₂O; 1 mol H₂ leftover.

misconception.wrong: The reactant with the smaller initial mole amount is always limiting.
misconception.why: Coefficients represent required ratios; absolute mole count alone is insufficient.
misconception.repair: Normalize each initial amount by its balanced coefficient.

demands.title: Normalize by coefficients
demands.core1a_explanation: Compare available moles per reaction set, not raw counts.
demands.worked_reasoning: For 2A+B→products, nA=3, nB=2 gives extents 1.5 and 2; A is limiting.
hints: Write a ledger for the chemical species and units given.
Check the balanced reaction and identify exactly which quantity is conserved.
Identify the bridging mole quantity; leave the final route selection to yourself.

core1b.model_response: A allows 6/3=2 units; B allows 3/2=1.5 units. B limits, so 1.5 mol C can form in the ideal equation.

demands.core1a_explanation: The extent fixes every amount consumed or produced in a single specified reaction.
demands.worked_reasoning: In 2H₂+O₂→2H₂O with nH₂=5 and nO₂=2, extent=2 gives 4 mol water, leaves 1 mol H₂.

core1b.reconstruct: Recreate the amount-of-substance ledger and explain every conversion or reaction relation.

core1b.model_response: Extent min(2/1,3/2)=1.5 mol; C=4.5 mol; A consumed 1.5, leftover 0.5 mol.

demands.title: Reverse limiting problem
demands.core1a_explanation: A product count plus leftover data can constrain initial composition; deductions depend on correct reaction identity.
demands.worked_reasoning: Given a completed 2H₂+O₂ reaction, water amount 4 mol and leftover H₂ 1 mol imply initial H₂=5 mol, O₂ at least 2 mol; without leftover O₂ measurement its initial amount is not uniquely fixed.
hints: Write a ledger for the chemical species and units given.
Check the balanced reaction and identify exactly which quantity is conserved.
Identify the bridging mole quantity; leave the final route selection to yourself.

core1b.predict: Predict the relevant ratio or limiting quantity and record the assumptions.
core1b.attempt: A completed ideal H₂/O₂ reaction produces 2 mol H₂O, leaves 1 mol O₂ and no H₂. Find both starting mole amounts.
core1b.reconstruct: Recreate the amount-of-substance ledger and explain every conversion or reaction relation.
core1b.diagnose: Assess whether this tempting approach would fail: Final product mass alone determines every initial reactant amount
core1b.repair: Use measured leftovers to close the remaining degrees of freedom.
core1b.boundary: If the leftover O₂ were not measured, would initial O₂ be uniquely known?
core1b.model_response: 2 mol water consumed 2 mol H₂ and 1 mol O₂. With no H₂ leftover, initial H₂=2 mol. O₂ initial = consumed 1+leftover 1=2 mol.

subtopics.source_notes: EXTENSION: deliberately beyond simple coefficient matching.

deep_dive.big_idea: A limiting-reagent calculation can be understood as a recipe constrained by amounts of chemically specified ingredients. However, the chemical 'recipe' must be balanced first, and the maximum product predicted from it is not automatically the product a real laboratory will collect.
reasoning_path: Write available reagent amounts in moles and divide each by its coefficient in the balanced equation.
Take the smallest resulting reaction extent under the ideal single-reaction assumptions.
Multiply the selected extent by every product and reagent coefficient to obtain theoretical final amounts.
Subtract reacted quantities from initial inventory to calculate excess reagent; then check conservation and nonnegative leftovers.

discovery.title: Which reagent runs out?
discovery.setup: For 2H₂+O₂→2H₂O, a model starts with 5 mol hydrogen and 2 mol oxygen in a controlled hypothetical closed reaction.
discovery.predict: Can all five moles of hydrogen react, given that only two moles of oxygen molecules are available?
discovery.observation: Two moles O₂ can consume four moles H₂ and generate four moles H₂O, leaving one mole H₂.
discovery.interpretation: Oxygen limits the ideal reaction extent; the other reagent may remain unreacted.
discovery.limits: This is an EXTENSION calculation and does not establish that the reaction truly reaches completion or that the gases may be safely mixed.

deep_dive.connection: A practical experiment often collects less product than the ideal ledger predicts, which introduces yield.

subtopics.title: Yield and multireaction stoichiometry (extension)
subtopics.entry_question: If the balanced equation predicts 10 g product, why might an experiment recover only 7 g?
core1a_paragraphs: The theoretical yield is the maximum amount of the target product predicted from the limiting reactant under the specified stoichiometric model. Actual isolated product may be lower due to incomplete conversion, side reactions or recovery losses.

Percent yield is commonly defined as actual isolated target-product mass divided by theoretical target-product mass, multiplied by 100. It is meaningful only when the compared products refer to the same chemical species and purity basis.

Multistage syntheses connect several material balances. Loss in one stage changes the reactant available to the next; multiplying independent stage yields is valid only under corresponding proportional-yield assumptions.
subtopics.representation: Use a flow diagram reactant → theoretical target → actual recovered target, with waste and recovery-loss arrows. Each arrow carries an explicit mass basis.

worked_example.problem: A stoichiometric reaction predicts 12 g product; experiment isolates 9 g of pure target.
steps: Define theoretical target product mass =12 g.
Define actual isolated pure target product mass =9 g.
worked_example.check: 0≤ yield≤100% under ordinary valid definitions; apparent >100% signals impurity or basis error.

misconception.wrong: Any lower mass proves the chemistry failed completely.
misconception.why: Incomplete conversion and physical collection losses are different mechanisms.
misconception.repair: Separate chemical conversion from isolated-product recovery.

demands.title: Yield with correct species basis
demands.core1a_explanation: An actual/theoretical comparison requires compatible chemical identity and purity bases.
demands.worked_reasoning: If 20 g theoretical and 15 g pure actual, yield 75%. A wet product measured at 18 g can overstate recovered pure mass.
hints: Write a ledger for the chemical species and units given.
Check the balanced reaction and identify exactly which quantity is conserved.
Identify the bridging mole quantity; leave the final route selection to yourself.

core1b.predict: Predict the relevant ratio or limiting quantity and record the assumptions.
core1b.attempt: A 16 g theoretical sample gives 12 g dry purified product. Find percent yield.
core1b.reconstruct: Recreate the amount-of-substance ledger and explain every conversion or reaction relation.
core1b.diagnose: Assess whether this tempting approach would fail: Use the reactant mass as denominator for yield
core1b.repair: Compare masses of the same target product.
core1b.boundary: What happens if the product sample contains 2 g solvent?
core1b.model_response: 12/16×100 =75%. Product identity and dryness are assumed independently verified.

demands.title: Differentiate reaction from recovery
demands.core1a_explanation: Two pathways can lower isolated yield: conversion inefficiency and collection inefficiency. Data from only final mass may not distinguish them.
demands.worked_reasoning: A reaction could produce 10 g target but lose 3 g on filtration, or chemically produce 7 g and collect all; final 7 g is shared.
demands.independent_check: Do not claim mechanism from net yield alone.
hints: Write a ledger for the chemical species and units given.
Check the balanced reaction and identify exactly which quantity is conserved.
Identify the bridging mole quantity; leave the final route selection to yourself.

core1b.predict: Predict the relevant ratio or limiting quantity and record the assumptions.
core1b.attempt: A 10 g theoretical experiment isolates 7 g. Does the measurement alone prove 30% unreacted reactant?
core1b.reconstruct: Recreate the amount-of-substance ledger and explain every conversion or reaction relation.
core1b.diagnose: Assess whether this tempting approach would fail: All missing target mass equals unreacted starting mass
core1b.repair: List distinct loss channels and design independent measurements.
core1b.boundary: How would measuring leftover reactant help?
core1b.model_response: No. Material may be lost in separation, converted to side products or left unreacted. Additional chemical analyses are required to attribute the 3 g gap.

demands.title: Two-stage effective yield
demands.core1a_explanation: Sequential stages with independent proportional retention multiply their yield fractions; this is a conditional model.
demands.worked_reasoning: If stage 1 yields 80% of theoretical and stage 2 converts 50% of stage-1 available material to a mass-scaled target, overall fraction is 0.8×0.5=0.4 relative to the appropriate theoretical baseline.
demands.independent_check: Check dimensional basis and factor multiplication.
hints: Write a ledger for the chemical species and units given.
Check the balanced reaction and identify exactly which quantity is conserved.
Identify the bridging mole quantity; leave the final route selection to yourself.

core1b.predict: Predict the relevant ratio or limiting quantity and record the assumptions.
core1b.attempt: An ideal route could give 25 g final product from initial input. Stage 1 operates at 80% and stage 2 at 60% of its stage-specific theoretical outcome. Under proportional assumptions, what final mass is expected?
core1b.reconstruct: Recreate the amount-of-substance ledger and explain every conversion or reaction relation.
core1b.diagnose: Assess whether this tempting approach would fail: Average 80% and 60% to get the overall yield
core1b.repair: Apply the second fraction to the reduced amount from stage 1.
core1b.boundary: Would doubling only the stage-2 yield double final output?
core1b.model_response: 25×0.8×0.6=12 g final product. The calculation requires that the ideal 25 g basis and sequential proportional yields are defined consistently.

subtopics.source_notes: EXTENSION, not an asserted compulsory Class X topic.

deep_dive.big_idea: Theoretical yield and actual isolated yield answer different questions. The first is a conservation-based maximum under the specified reaction model; the second is a measurement that also depends on conversion, competing reactions, recovery and purity. Their ratio is informative only if both refer to the same target product.
reasoning_path: Use the balanced reaction and limiting reactant to determine the maximum target product under ideal conditions.
State what the measured product actually includes: wet crystals, solvent or by-products can artificially inflate an apparent mass.
Calculate percent yield only after using an appropriately purified target-product mass.
For a multistage process, carry forward the quantity actually available after each stage rather than applying unrelated percentage shortcuts.

discovery.title: A missing-mass investigation
discovery.setup: A thought experiment predicts 12 g pure target product theoretically, but only 9 g dry material is isolated.
discovery.predict: Does that result establish that exactly 3 g of starting reactant failed to react?
discovery.observation: The isolated yield is 75%, but multiple causes—unreacted reagent, side reactions or transfer losses—could explain the shortfall.
discovery.interpretation: An outcome measurement does not uniquely diagnose its mechanism without additional analyses.
discovery.limits: Yield modelling is marked EXTENSION; meaningful interpretation requires verified product purity and clearly specified reaction conditions.

deep_dive.connection: This quantitative discipline becomes a prerequisite when Agent B develops C08 reactions, C09 neutralisation and C13 redox analysis.

chapter_spine.central_question: How can a balance in grams tell us how many invisible reacting entities are present, and which chemical amounts can be formed?
prior_knowledge: C03 chemical formulas, atom conservation and valency
Distinguishing a sample mass from amount of substance
journey: Define a mole using specified entities
Translate mass to amount to particle count
Read balanced equations as mole relations
Calculate products from a correct reaction ledger
Extend to limiting reactants and actual yields only under declared scope
chapter_spine.chapter_closure: Every quantitative reaction solution must show the unit counted, the correct species formula, balanced coefficients, a conservation ledger and a statement of model conditions. Numerical plausibility is not enough without chemical identity.

key_terms.mole: SI amount of substance containing exactly 6.02214076×10²³ specified entities.
key_terms.molar_mass: Mass per mole of a specified chemical entity.
key_terms.stoichiometry: Quantitative relation among reacting and produced chemical entities.
key_terms.limiting_reactant: Reactant that sets the maximum progress of a specified ideal reaction.
key_terms.theoretical_yield: Ideal product amount predicted from stoichiometric constraints.
key_terms.actual_yield: Measured amount of target product collected under specified experimental conditions.
